summary: This opinion piece argues that philanthropists, policymakers and employers should prioritize financial aid and scholarships for adult learners, who face stagnant wages, rising living costs and debt. It uses the stories of Marianne Vasquez and Raj Patel, economic arguments, and a rebuttal of myths about adult learners. It also lists new aid initiatives since September 2023 and recommends tax breaks, expanded federal aid and a cultural shift toward lifelong learning.
one_line: An opinion essay arguing that scholarships, grants, employer programs and policy changes should expand financial aid for adult learners returning to education.
key_facts: Adult learners juggle work, family and financial burdens; stagnant wages, rising living costs and preexisting debt are major barriers to further education.
Marianne Vasquez, a 45-year-old single mother of two working two jobs, enrolled in college in October 2023 thanks to a local scholarship aimed at adult learners.
Raj Patel, a 38-year-old automotive technician, received a need-based grant for adult students that enabled his transition toward renewable energy engineering.
The author argues adults who return to school are more likely to land higher-paying jobs, boosting consumer spending and the tax base.
The author counters the myth that adults benefit less from education, claiming they often have higher course completion rates and apply skills immediately at work.
The state government unveiled a 'Second Chance' grant program in early November that promises to waive tuition fees for adults completing post-secondary education.
The Anderson Foundation, led by philanthropist James Anderson, committed $5 million in scholarship funds for adults over age 30 returning to college or vocational training.
Metro City Community College launched the 'Back to School' fund in December 2023, offering micro-scholarships covering textbooks and ancillary fees for returning adults.
TechForward's 'Learn and Earn' program, conceptualized by HR Director Sandra Jeffries, gives employees flexible schedules and partial tuition reimbursement in partnership with local colleges.
The author recommends tax breaks for businesses supporting employee continuing education and expanded federal financial aid that recognizes adult learners' circumstances.
The author calls for a cultural shift and for marketing campaigns, success stories and community outreach that put adults front and center.
The article ends with a heading on access to education as a moral imperative and right, but the section text is not included.
